content: Nafcillin is an antibiotic that is effective against specific bacterial infections. It is not suitable for treating viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus, nor is it effective against non-bacterial infections. Using nafcillin or any antibiotic unnecessarily, such as for non-bacterial infections or when no infection is present, can lead to antibiotic resistance, making it less effective in the future. Nafcillin may also be prescribed for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. Nafcillin works by killing certain bacteria through the inhibition of their ability to form a protective cell wall, which is essential for their survival. Nafcillin is available in injectable forms, including 1 g, 2 g, 10 g, 20 mg/mL, and 2 g/100 mL injections. It is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. The most common side effects of nafcillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site, as well as rashes. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. Serious side effects, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, liver damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and blood disorders. Symptoms of severe allergic reactions may include difficulty breathing, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting. If you experience any of these, seek immediate medical attention. Seizures have been reported in some individuals using nafcillin. Signs of a seizure may include muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, stiffening of the arms or legs, confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. If you suspect a seizure, stop using nafcillin and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Nafcillin can also cause kidney damage, with symptoms such as reduced urination, swelling in the feet or legs, unusual tiredness, chest pain, confusion, or nausea. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, may present as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). If you notice any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider promptly. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), can occur during or up to two months after stopping nafcillin. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience these symptoms. Nafcillin may also lead to blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, neutropenia, or bone marrow depression. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual tiredness, dizziness, or an abnormal heartbeat. If you experience these, stop using nafcillin and seek medical attention immediately. Certain individuals should not use nafcillin, including those allergic to nafcillin, its ingredients, or other penicillin-based medications. Inform your healthcare provider if you have asthma, liver disease, kidney disease, a history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, or allergies to corn or corn products. Additionally, discuss any prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or supplements you are taking, as nafcillin may interact with other drugs, such as tetracyclines, warfarin, cyclosporine, or probenecid. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your healthcare provider, as nafcillin passes into breast milk, and its effects on pregnancy are not fully known. There are no known interactions between nafcillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption may weaken your immune response, making it harder for your body to fight infections. In the event of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a poison control center. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is close to the time for your next dose. Do not double doses. It is important to complete the full course of nafcillin as prescribed, even if symptoms improve, to prevent antibiotic resistance. Nafcillin is primarily used to treat bacterial infections but may not be effective for all types of bacteria, as some may have developed resistance. Always use antibiotics responsibly and under the guidance of a healthcare provider.
